title: The Letter to the Ephesians
subtitle: Pros Ephesious, “To the Ephesians”
description: Paul’s letter of the church, written in chains and probably carried from one congregation of Asia to the next. It opens in a long outpouring of praise for every blessing in Christ, prays for eyes to see it, and tells Gentile readers who were once dead in their trespasses that God, rich in mercy, has made them alive: “it is by this grace that you have been saved, through faith.” Christ has broken down the wall between Jew and Gentile and made one new humanity, a body, a household, a temple; and so the letter turns to how such a people lives, in unity and truth, as children of light filled by the Spirit, in marriage and household, and armoured in God’s strength. In the Open Word Bible, a new translation from the Greek given freely to the public domain, with an introduction to the letter’s shape and meaning and a conclusion on where to read next.

qa.question: What is the Letter to the Ephesians?
qa.answer: The tenth book of the New Testament, a letter of the apostle Paul to the Christians of Ephesus and probably of other churches in the Roman province of Asia. Its first three chapters praise God for what he has done in Christ: choosing and redeeming his people, raising the spiritually dead to life by grace, and making Jews and Gentiles into one body. Its last three chapters show how that people is to live, beginning with the call to “live in a way that is worthy of God’s call” (4:1).

qa.question: Who wrote Ephesians, and when?
qa.answer: The letter names the apostle Paul as its author and speaks of him as a prisoner (3:1; 4:1; 6:20). The church has always received it as his, usually dated to his imprisonment in Rome around AD 60–62, when Tychicus carried it together with Colossians (6:21–22). Many modern scholars think it was written after Paul’s death by a disciple who knew his letters well, pointing to its style and its close dependence on Colossians; many others defend Paul’s authorship. Either way it gathers up his gospel as a whole.

qa.question: Was Ephesians written to the church in Ephesus?
qa.answer: Probably to Ephesus and beyond. Paul spent about three years in Ephesus (Acts 20:31), yet the letter sends no personal greetings and speaks of the readers’ faith as something he has heard about (1:15). Some of the oldest manuscripts lack the words “in Ephesus” in 1:1, and in the second century Marcion called it the letter to the Laodiceans. Many readers think it was a circular letter for the churches of Asia, with Ephesus as the chief among them.

qa.question: What does Ephesians 2:8–9 mean by being saved by grace through faith?
qa.answer: That salvation is God’s free gift and not a reward for anything we have done: “None of this comes from you; it is God’s gift,” and so “there is no room for anyone to boast.” Paul has just described his readers as dead in their trespasses and made alive by a God rich in mercy. But he goes straight on to say that God created us in Christ Jesus “for good works” (2:10), so that grace is the root of a changed life, not a substitute for one.

qa.question: What does Ephesians teach about wives and husbands?
qa.answer: Ephesians 5:21–33 calls believers to submit to one another in the reverent fear of Christ, asks wives to submit to their husbands as to the Lord, and asks husbands to love their wives the way Christ loved the church and handed himself over for her. Paul says marriage points to “Christ and the church” (5:32). Christians differ over how to apply it: some see the husband’s self-giving headship as a lasting pattern, others see mutual submission as the governing idea, transforming the household customs of Paul’s day from within.

qa.question: Which translation of the Bible is this?
qa.answer: The Open Word Bible, a new translation made directly from the Greek and dedicated to the public domain, printed here at its Balanced level, which aims to be accurate and to read naturally aloud. The reasoning behind each of its sentences, with the Greek beside it, is published at openwordbible.org. The introduction and conclusion were written for this edition.
